functions.yields: Adjusted R² as a scalar, typically in [0, 1] but can be negative
functions.description:
Adjusted R² penalises R² for the number of predictors relative to sample size, correcting for the inflation that occurs when irrelevant predictors are added. It equals 1 - (1 - R²) × df_total / df_residual, which reduces to the familiar 1 - (1 - R²)(n-1)/(n-k-1) when an intercept is fit. Unlike R² it can decrease when a predictor adds less explanatory power than expected by chance, and can be negative when the model fits worse than a horizontal line.

Computed as 1 - (1 - R_squared(...)) * DF_Total(...) / DF_Residual(...), inheriting the Allow_Intercept correction from both df functions.
functions.plain_language_summary: R-squared adjusted so extra predictors do not get free credit.

=LAMBDA(X_s, Y, [Allow_Intercept], [Filter],

    h,         Hat_diagonal(X_s, allow_arg, filt_arg),

functions.yields: PRESS (Prediction Residual Error Sum of Squares) as a scalar
functions.description:
PRESS is the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) sum of squared prediction errors. For each observation i the model is refitted on all other observations and evaluated at x_i; the shortcut formula avoids n separate refits by computing Σ(eᵢ / (1 − hᵢ))² where eᵢ are the OLS residuals and hᵢ are the hat-matrix diagonal (leverage) values.

Leverage is obtained from Hat_diagonal, which delegates the matrix inversion to Gram_Inverse. Then SUMSQ(e / (1 − h)) gives PRESS as a scalar.
functions.plain_language_summary: How well the model predicts rows it did not get to train on.

functions.yields: Durbin-Watson statistic as a scalar
functions.description:
DW = Σ(eₜ − eₜ₋₁)² / Σeₜ², testing for first-order serial correlation in residuals. Values near 2 indicate no autocorrelation; values below ~1.5 suggest positive autocorrelation, values above ~2.5 suggest negative autocorrelation.

Computed as SUM((DROP(e,1) − DROP(e,−1))²) / SUM(e²), where DROP(e,1) removes the first residual (giving e₂..eₙ) and DROP(e,−1) removes the last (giving e₁..eₙ₋₁), so consecutive differences are formed without OFFSET or index arithmetic.
functions.plain_language_summary: Whether nearby residuals tend to move together instead of staying independent.

Variance Inflation Factor for each predictor Xⱼ = 1 / (1 − R²ⱼ), where R²ⱼ is the R² from regressing Xⱼ on all other predictors. VIF measures how much the variance of coefficient j is inflated by multicollinearity. VIF = 1 means no collinearity; VIF > 10 (or > 5 by stricter convention) signals a problem.

functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(X_s, Y, X_new, [Allow_Intercept], [Filter], [alpha],
  LET(
    allow_arg,     IF(ISOMITTED(Allow_Intercept), TRUE, Allow_Intercept),
    filt_arg,      IF(ISOMITTED(Filter),          TRUE, Filter),
    alpha_arg,     IF(ISOMITTED(alpha),           0.05, alpha),
    X_design,      Design_Matrix(X_s, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    beta,          Coefficients(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    s,             SE_Regression(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    df,            DF_Residual(X_s, Y, allow_arg, filt_arg),
    t_crit,        T.INV.2T(alpha_arg, df),
    x_new_aligned, IF(allow_arg, X_new, INDEX(X_new, SEQUENCE(ROWS(X_new) - 1, 1, 2, 1))),
    XtX_inv,       Gram_Inverse(X_design),
    h_new,         MMULT(MMULT(TRANSPOSE(x_new_aligned), XtX_inv), x_new_aligned),
    point_est,     SUMPRODUCT(x_new_aligned, beta),
    se_pred,       s * SQRT(1 + h_new),
    margin,        t_crit * se_pred,
    VSTACK(
      point_est,
      se_pred,
      t_crit,
      point_est - margin,
      point_est + margin,
      1 - alpha_arg
    )
  ))

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of Pearson correlations between each predictor and Y
functions.description:
Pearson_R computes the linear (Pearson product-moment) correlation between each column of X_s and Y, after applying the optional filter. When X_s has a single column the result is a scalar; when X_s has k columns it spills as a k×1 column vector.

A Pearson_R close to ±1 indicates a strong linear association. Comparing Pearson_R with Spearman_R on the same data reveals nonlinearity: a large gap (Spearman > Pearson in magnitude) suggests a monotonic but curved relationship that may warrant a log or polynomial transformation.
functions.plain_language_summary: The straight-line relationship between each predictor and the outcome.

functions.name: Spearman_R
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(xf, yf, [Filter],
  LET(
    baseFilter, IF(ISOMITTED(Filter), TRUE, Filter),
    RankAvgAsc, LAMBDA(a,
      MAP(a, LAMBDA(v, 1+SUM(--(a<v))+(SUM(--(a=v))-1)/2))
    ),
    TRANSPOSE(
      BYCOL(xf,
        LAMBDA(xcol,
          LET(
            valid, baseFilter*ISNUMBER(xcol)*ISNUMBER(yf),
            x, FILTER(xcol, valid),
            y, FILTER(yf, valid),
            rx, RankAvgAsc(x),
            ry, RankAvgAsc(y),
            CORREL(rx, ry)
          )
        )
      )
    )
  ))

arguments.description: single-column outcome range

arguments.name: Filter
arguments.description: boolean array — TRUE includes the row, FALSE excludes it

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of Spearman rank correlations between each predictor and Y
functions.description:
Spearman_R computes the rank (Spearman) correlation between each column of xf and yf. For each predictor column, rows are kept where both that column and yf are numeric (and pass the optional Filter). Ties receive average ranks via a MAP-based helper (avoids RANK.AVG on dynamic arrays). Returns a k×1 vector when xf has k columns.

Unlike Pearson_R, Spearman_R measures any monotonic relationship, not just linear ones. The diagnostic value of the pair is in their difference: if |Spearman_R| is noticeably larger than |Pearson_R| for the same predictor, the relationship is curved and a transformation (e.g. LOG) or a nonlinear term may improve model fit.

functions.description:
Skewness returns the sample skewness (Fisher-Pearson standardized third moment) for each column of X_s after filtering. Uses Excel's SKEW function, which divides by (n-1)(n-2).

Interpretation: 0 = symmetric; positive = right tail (mean > median, common in counts and incomes); negative = left tail. |Skewness| > 1 typically signals that a log or square-root transformation would linearize relationships and stabilize regression residual variance. Compare with Kurtosis for a fuller picture of distributional shape.

functions.description:
Kurtosis returns the excess kurtosis for each filtered column of X_s. Uses Excel's KURT function (Fisher's excess kurtosis: kurtosis − 3, so a normal distribution returns 0).

Positive excess kurtosis (leptokurtic) indicates heavier tails and more extreme outliers than a normal distribution. Negative (platykurtic) indicates lighter tails. High kurtosis in a predictor or in regression residuals signals that OLS standard errors may be unreliable, and that robust standard errors or a different distributional assumption may be warranted.
functions.plain_language_summary: Whether a variable has unusually heavy tails or outliers.

functions.yields: F-statistic for the overall regression model as a scalar
functions.description:
F_Stat returns the F-statistic for the omnibus test of the null hypothesis that all regression coefficients are simultaneously zero. It equals (MS_Regression / MS_Residual) = (SS_Regression / df_regression) / (SS_Residual / df_residual).

A large F-statistic (and correspondingly small P_Value_F) means the model explains significantly more variance than would be expected by chance. Note that a significant F does not guarantee that every individual predictor is significant — individual t-statistics (T_Stats) address that question. F_Stat appears in the ANOVA table on the Regression sheet; this function exposes it as a named reference for use in other formulas.
functions.plain_language_summary: Whether the model, taken as a whole, explains more than random noise would.

      DF_Regression(X_s),

P_Value_F returns the p-value for the overall model F-test: the probability of observing an F-statistic at least as large as F_Stat under the null hypothesis that all coefficients are zero. Computed as F.DIST.RT(F_Stat, df_regression, df_residual).

Conventionally, P_Value_F < 0.05 indicates that the model as a whole fits the data significantly better than a null model. This p-value appears in the Significance F column of the Regression sheet ANOVA table; this function exposes it for programmatic use.

Use this to screen for multicollinearity before fitting a model: pairs with |r| > 0.7 are candidates for VIF investigation. High off-diagonal correlations indicate redundant predictors whose coefficients will be unstable and hard to interpret. For formal post-fit diagnostics, use VIF and Tolerance instead.

functions.name: Sturges_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    CEILING(LOG(n, 2) + 1, 1)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via Sturges' rule
functions.description:
Sturges_Bins returns the bin count k = ⌈log₂(n) + 1⌉, where n is the count of numeric values after filtering. Sturges' rule works well for roughly symmetric, unimodal data with moderate sample sizes (50–200 observations). It tends to undersmooth (too few bins) for skewed or heavy-tailed data.

Used by Bin_Edges to generate upper bin edges for the Sturges histogram column chart.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins Sturges' rule recommends for this data.

functions.name: Scott_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    sd, STDEV.S(x),
    width, 3.49 * sd * n ^ (-1/3),
    range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
    CEILING(range_ / width, 1)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via Scott's normal reference rule
functions.description:
Scott_Bins computes the bin width h = 3.49 × σ × n^(−1/3) that minimises mean integrated squared error assuming the data are normally distributed, then returns k = ⌈range / h⌉.

Scott's rule is more adaptive than Sturges for larger samples and performs well when the data are approximately normal. For strongly skewed or multimodal data, Freedman-Diaconis is more appropriate.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins Scott's normal-reference rule recommends.

functions.name: FD_Bins
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    n, COUNT(x),
    iqr, QUARTILE.EXC(x, 3) - QUARTILE.EXC(x, 1),
    width, 2 * iqr * n ^ (-1/3),
    range_, MAX(x) - MIN(x),
    CEILING(range_ / width, 1)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array

functions.yields: integer bin count via the Freedman-Diaconis rule
functions.description:
FD_Bins computes the bin width h = 2 × IQR × n^(−1/3) where IQR is the interquartile range (QUARTILE.EXC), then returns k = ⌈range / h⌉.

Freedman-Diaconis is robust to outliers because it uses the IQR rather than the standard deviation. It is the preferred rule for skewed or heavy-tailed distributions and for large samples where the shape deviates from normality.
functions.plain_language_summary: How many histogram bins the Freedman-Diaconis rule recommends.

functions.name: Bin_Edges
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, method, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    min_x, MIN(x),
    max_x, MAX(x),
    k, IF(method = "Sturges", Sturges_Bins(data, filt_arg),
         IF(method = "Scott",   Scott_Bins(data,   filt_arg),
            FD_Bins(data, filt_arg))),
    width, (max_x - min_x) / k,
    SEQUENCE(k, 1, min_x + width, width)
  ))

arguments.description: single-column numeric data range

arguments.name: method
arguments.description: bin-count method: "Sturges", "Scott", or "FD"

arguments.name: filter

functions.yields: k×1 column vector of upper bin edges (evenly spaced from min to max)
functions.description:
Bin_Edges returns a column vector of upper bin edges using the specified bin-count rule. Edges are evenly spaced from min+width to max (half-open (lower, upper] intervals matching Excel's FREQUENCY and histogram-chart convention). The vector length equals the bin count from the chosen method.

Pass the output directly to Bin_Counts. Use the spill range (e.g. F4#) as the chart category axis. The bin width equals (max − min) / k regardless of the rule — the rule determines only k.

  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),

functions.description:
NLL_Normal computes −Σ ln f(xᵢ | μ, σ) where f is the Normal PDF evaluated via NORM.DIST. Minimising NLL over (μ, σ) gives the MLE; for the Normal distribution the MLE is the sample mean and sample standard deviation.

The filter defaults to ISNUMBER(data) so blank cells in the input range are automatically excluded. Pass this value to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 2.
functions.plain_language_summary: How unlikely the Normal distribution is to have generated this data at the given parameters.

functions.name: NLL_Triangular
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, min_val, mode_val, max_val, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    range_, max_val - min_val,
    pdf, IF(
      x <= mode_val,
      2 * (x - min_val)  / (range_ * (mode_val - min_val)),
      2 * (max_val - x)  / (range_ * (max_val - mode_val))
    ),
    IFERROR(-SUMPRODUCT(LN(pdf)), 1E+15)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: min_val
arguments.description: lower bound of the triangular distribution

arguments.name: mode_val
arguments.description: peak (most likely value)

arguments.name: max_val
arguments.description: upper bound

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: negative log-likelihood for Triangular(min, mode, max) given data; returns 1E+15 for invalid parameters
functions.description:
NLL_Triangular implements the triangular PDF directly: 2(x − min) / (range × (mode − min)) on [min, mode] and 2(max − x) / (range × (max − mode)) on (mode, max]. The likelihood is non-differentiable at the mode, so MLE is non-standard; the conventional approach is to set min = data min, mode = data mode, max = data max.

Triangular is common in project risk and cost estimation (three-point estimates). Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 3.
functions.plain_language_summary: How unlikely the Triangular distribution is to have generated this data at the given bounds.

functions.description:
NLL_Beta evaluates −Σ ln f(xᵢ | α, β) via BETA.DIST. Values exactly at 0 or 1 cause BETA.DIST to return errors; the IFERROR sentinel catches these and maps the entire NLL to 1E+15, making the cell visible as an overflow region in grid-search heatmaps.

Beta fits proportions and rates bounded on [0, 1] (e.g. efficiencies, fractions). Data must be rescaled to (0, 1) before fitting. No closed-form MLE; fit using grid-search Data Table (v2.1). Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 2.
functions.plain_language_summary: How unlikely the Beta distribution is to have generated this (0,1)-bounded data at the given shape parameters.

functions.name: NLL_BetaPERT
functions.formula_display:
=LAMBDA(data, min_val, mode_val, max_val, [filter],
  LET(
    filt_arg, IF(ISOMITTED(filter), ISNUMBER(data), filter),
    x, FILTER(data, filt_arg),
    range_, max_val - min_val,
    z, (x - min_val) / range_,
    alpha_p, 1 + 4 * (mode_val - min_val) / range_,
    beta_p,  1 + 4 * (max_val  - mode_val) / range_,
    pdf_z, BETA.DIST(z, alpha_p, beta_p, FALSE),
    pdf_x, pdf_z / range_,
    IFERROR(-SUMPRODUCT(LN(pdf_x)), 1E+15)
  ))

arguments.name: data
arguments.description: single-column data range

arguments.name: min_val
arguments.description: lower bound (minimum possible value)

arguments.name: mode_val
arguments.description: most likely value (peak of the PERT curve)

arguments.name: max_val
arguments.description: upper bound (maximum possible value)

arguments.name: filter
arguments.description: optional boolean array; defaults to ISNUMBER(data)

functions.yields: negative log-likelihood for BetaPERT(min, mode, max) given data; returns 1E+15 for invalid parameters
functions.description:
NLL_BetaPERT reparameterises the Beta distribution using the PERT convention: α = 1 + 4·(mode − min)/(max − min), β = 1 + 4·(max − mode)/(max − min). Data are rescaled to z = (x − min)/(max − min); the Jacobian correction log(1/(max − min)) converts the Beta log-likelihood back to the original data scale.

BetaPERT is the standard distribution for three-point cost and schedule estimates. Parameters are estimated directly from min, mode, max; no optimisation is needed. Pass to GoF_AIC and GoF_BIC with k = 3.
functions.plain_language_summary: How unlikely the BetaPERT distribution is to have generated this data at the given three-point bounds.

functions.name: GoF_AIC
functions.formula_display: =LAMBDA(nll, k, 2 * k + 2 * nll)

arguments.name: nll
arguments.description: negative log-likelihood from any NLL_* function

arguments.name: k
arguments.description: number of free parameters in the distribution (1 for Exponential, 2 for Normal/Lognormal/Weibull/Gamma/Beta, 3 for Triangular/BetaPERT)

functions.yields: AIC = 2k + 2·NLL as a scalar
functions.description:
GoF_AIC computes the Akaike Information Criterion: AIC = 2k + 2·NLL. Lower AIC indicates a better balance of fit quality and model complexity. AIC is comparable across all distributions fitted to the same dataset — the distribution with the lowest AIC is the best-fitting model under this criterion.

AIC does not penalise extra parameters as strongly as BIC, so it may favour more complex distributions (larger k) when sample sizes are large. For small samples, use AICc instead (not implemented here — add a correction term 2k(k+1)/(n−k−1) if n/k < 40).
functions.plain_language_summary: A model-comparison score that balances fit quality against the number of parameters.

functions.name: GoF_BIC
functions.formula_display: =LAMBDA(nll, k, n, k * LN(n) + 2 * nll)

arguments.name: nll
arguments.description: negative log-likelihood from any NLL_* function

arguments.name: k
arguments.description: number of free parameters in the distribution

arguments.name: n
arguments.description: number of observations used in the fit (from UV_n or COUNT(data))

functions.yields: BIC = k·ln(n) + 2·NLL as a scalar
functions.description:
GoF_BIC computes the Bayesian Information Criterion: BIC = k·ln(n) + 2·NLL. Lower BIC indicates a better model. BIC penalises extra parameters more strongly than AIC (penalty grows with log(n) rather than 2), favouring simpler distributions in larger samples.

Compare AIC and BIC together: if they agree, the best-fit distribution is clear; if they disagree, AIC is selecting a more complex distribution and BIC is selecting a simpler one. The difference is informative about how much the extra parameters contribute to fit.
functions.plain_language_summary: A model-comparison score that penalises extra parameters more strongly as sample size grows.
